passages.text: 一局游戏，是怎样一步步发生的？
小林把一只小兔棋子放在纸上，小雨把小刺猬放在它旁边。两只动物面前是一条河。小林伸手想把小兔直接放到对岸，小雨却说：“先等等，它能一下子跳过去吗？”
这就是我们开始理解游戏的地方。纸上的动物可以被手拿到任何地方，但这一局允许怎样移动，需要大家先说好。接下来，我们跟着一个为讲解编写的小例子，看他们怎样开始、怎样继续，又在什么时候停下。你只需跟着文字读，不用准备棋子。
先知道要去哪里
这条河只有一条路线：起点岸，第一块踏脚石，第二块踏脚石，最后是对岸。两只动物都从起点出发，只能向前走到相邻的位置，不能跳格，也不能退回去。它们可以站在同一块石头上，不会挡住彼此。
小林负责小兔，小雨负责小刺猬。他们想让两只动物都到对岸，一只先到了还不算成功。桌子中央放着四块木板，两人共用；谁移动，都从这里取。每向前走一步就要用掉一块木板，表示临时搭桥。用过的木板放到一旁，这一局不能再拿回来使用。桌外另放十六块备用纸片，代表还没收集到的新木板；它们还不属于中央的可用木板。
现在，纸上的几样东西有了联系。小兔想前进，需要中央还有木板；小兔用掉一块，小刺猬接下来可用的就少了一块。只认识动物和木板的名称，还不够解释这局怎样玩。我们还要知道，一样东西的变化会怎样影响另一样东西。
轮到你，先做一件事
小林先行动，然后小雨行动。两人各行动一次，才算完成一轮；整局最多四轮。轮到一个人做事的这段机会，叫作他的“回合”。所以，一轮里有小林和小雨两个回合。
每个回合只能做一件事。你可以花一块木板，让自己的动物向前走一步。如果动物还在起点岸，也可以留在原地，从桌外的备用纸片中收集两块新木板，放进中央。你还可以等待，这次不移动，也不增加木板。木板不够时不能前进，离开起点后也不能再收集。
小雨若选择收集，不能紧接着又走一步；那要等下次轮到她。小兔到了对岸以后就留在那里，之后轮到小林时只能等待。两人可以商量，但各自决定自己动物的行动。
这些规定把一次动作的起点和终点说清了。我们知道谁能做、可以选什么、做完会改变什么，也知道什么时候该交给下一个人。
跟着两只动物走完四轮
第一轮，小林用一块木板，小兔走上第一块石头。中央从四块变成三块。小雨让小刺猬留在岸边，收集两块，中央便有五块。第一轮结束时，小兔走在前面，小刺猬还没出发，但两人可用的木板比刚才多了。
第二轮，两人都选择前进。小兔来到第二块石头，小刺猬来到第一块；各用掉一块，中央剩三块。
第三轮，小兔再用一块，抵达对岸。小刺猬也向前一步，来到第二块石头，中央还剩一块。小兔已经安全了，不过两人的目标还没完成：小刺猬也得过去。
第四轮，轮到小林，他让已经到岸的小兔等待。随后小雨用掉最后一块木板，小刺猬也抵达对岸。两只都到了，这局立刻结束，两人共同获胜。假如第四轮结束时还有一只没到，他们就会失败。
这里既有“什么时候停”，也有“怎样算成功”。只有小兔到了，不能提前宣布大家赢了；木板花光，也不一定失败——刚才最后一块恰好把最后一只动物送到了岸上。
下一步，取决于现在的局面
再看第一轮结束的那一刻：小兔在第一块石头，小刺猬在起点，中央有五块木板，已经过了一轮。这些会影响后续行动的信息，可以合起来叫“当前局面”，也可以简称为游戏的“状态”。
它不只是一个分数。小刺猬还在起点，意味着它仍能收集；小兔已经离岸，意味着它失去了这项做法。五块木板意味着接下来最多还能支付五次前进。已经用掉一轮，意味着每只动物最多还剩三次行动机会。
于是，游戏一边进行，下一步能做什么也一边改变。规则把这些变化接在一起；玩家再根据新的局面决定怎么做。设计者写下的不是一串必须照演的台词，而是大家据以行动的共同约定。
刚才我们走完的是一种成功办法。小雨第一轮为什么没有跟着小兔一起走？两个人都前进，看起来不是更快吗？这是一个值得留下的问题。接下来先学会怎样观察：我们确实看见了哪些动作，又给这些动作加上了什么解释。之后再回到这次选择，细看它怎样改变后面的路。
这款小游戏是为了把问题讲清而编写的起点。完整走得通，说明它的规则至少允许刚才这段过程；朋友会不会喜欢、愿不愿意再玩，还要继续了解。在后面的章节里，我们会从它出发，尝试自己的点子，并学会怎样检查一份新草稿。
How Does a Game Happen, One Move at a Time?

Lin places a Rabbit piece on a sheet of paper. Yu puts Hedgehog beside it. A river lies ahead. Lin reaches to put Rabbit straight on the far bank, but Yu stops him: “Wait—can it jump all the way across?”

This is a useful place to begin understanding games. A hand can put a piece anywhere. What the piece may do in this game depends on the rules everyone agrees to use. We will follow an invented example from its beginning to its end. You can follow it in the text; you do not need any pieces.
Know Where You Are Going

There is one route across the river: the starting bank, the first stepping stone, the second stepping stone, and the far bank. Both animals start on the starting bank. They can move only to the next position ahead, without skipping a position or going backward. They may share any position, so neither blocks the other.

Lin controls Rabbit and Yu controls Hedgehog. Their goal is to get both animals across. Getting just one across is not enough. Four planks lie in the middle of the table for them to share. Each step forward uses one plank to make a temporary bridge. Used planks are put aside and cannot be used again during this game. Another sixteen paper pieces sit outside the playing area as spare planks that have not yet been collected. They are not part of the available shared supply.

The objects now connect to one another. Rabbit needs a plank to move. When Rabbit uses one, Hedgehog has one fewer available. Knowing the names of the animals and the planks would not explain how this game works. We need to follow how a change to one affects the others.
On Your Turn, Do One Thing
Lin acts first, then Yu. Each person's opportunity to act is a turn. When both have taken a turn, one round is complete. The game lasts at most four rounds.

On a turn, you choose one thing to do. You may spend one shared plank to move your animal one position forward. If it is still on the starting bank, you may instead keep it there and collect two new planks from those spare pieces and add them to the shared supply. You may also wait, without moving or collecting anything. You cannot move without enough planks, and you cannot collect after leaving the starting bank.

If Yu collects, she cannot move immediately afterward; she must wait for her next turn. An animal that reaches the far bank stays there. Its player can only wait on later turns. The players may discuss their plans, but each decides their own animal's action.
These rules give an action a clear beginning and end. We know who can act, what they may choose, what changes afterward, and when the next person gets a turn.
Follow Both Animals Through Four Rounds

In the first round, Lin spends one plank and moves Rabbit onto the first stone. Three planks remain. Yu keeps Hedgehog on the starting bank and collects two, bringing the shared supply to five. Rabbit is ahead and Hedgehog has not left, but they now have more planks available.
In the second round, both move. Rabbit reaches the second stone; Hedgehog reaches the first. They each spend a plank, leaving three.

In the third round, Rabbit spends a plank to reach the far bank. Hedgehog also moves forward, reaching the second stone. One plank remains. Rabbit is safe, but their shared goal is still unfinished: Hedgehog must cross too.

In the fourth round, Lin waits with Rabbit on the far bank. Yu then spends the last plank to bring Hedgehog across. Both animals have arrived, so the game ends immediately with a shared win. If either animal had still been short of the far bank at the end of the fourth round, they would have lost.

The rules tell us both when to stop and what counts as success. Rabbit arriving alone does not mean they have won. Using the last plank does not necessarily mean failure, either: here, it took the last animal to the far bank.
What Comes Next Depends on What Is Here Now

Return to the end of the first round. Rabbit is on the first stone. Hedgehog is on the starting bank. Five planks remain, and one round has passed. Together, the information that matters to what can happen next forms the current situation, often called the game's state.

It includes more than a score. Hedgehog's position means it can still collect. Rabbit's position means it no longer can. Five planks can pay for five more forward moves. With one round used, each animal has at most three turns left.

As the game proceeds, what is possible next changes too. Rules connect these changes, and players decide what to do in the new situation. The designer has written a shared agreement for acting, rather than a script that everyone must perform word for word.

We have followed one way to succeed. Why did Yu stay behind in the first round? Wouldn't moving both animals forward have been faster? Keep that question. First, we will learn how to observe: which actions did we actually see, and what explanations have we added to them? Later we will return to this choice and examine how it changes the road ahead.

This little game was invented as a starting point for explaining design. Working through it shows that its rules allow the sequence we followed. Whether friends enjoy it or want to play again remains something to investigate. In the chapters ahead, we will use it to explore ideas of our own and learn how to check a new draft.
看过一局以后，究竟看到了什么？
第一轮，小林让小兔前进一步，中央木板从四块变成三块。轮到小雨，她让小刺猬留在起点，收集两块新木板，中央于是有了五块。一只动物走远了，另一只没有动。只看位置，很容易觉得小林在推进游戏，小雨在拖延。
可是，留下收集也改变了局面。两只动物总共要走六步，最初的四块木板不够。如果双方第一轮都前进，剩下的两块就无法支持后面的四步，而它们已经离开了唯一能收集的起点。位置和木板一起看，才看得出“没有移动”也可能帮助过河。
设计者观察游戏，首先要练习把这样的变化看完整。否则，很可能把“动物没动”误当成“这一回合没有作用”，接着增加一个根本不需要的新动作。
先把眼前发生的事说准
一句“他们合作得很好”已经包含了判断。相比之下，“小林移动后，中央剩三块；小雨选择收集，中央变成五块”让别人也能重建这个局面。接着可以记下当时说了什么、先做了什么、随后发生了什么。先后顺序很有用：小雨是在小林提醒后收集，还是自己先提出留下？这两种过程可能得到同样的木板数量，却给设计者留下不同的问题。
这里的先后差别只是两种假设，并不是已经发生的试玩。想象第一种过程，小林说“你别走，先拿木板”，小雨照做。我们能说他提出了安排，她采用了它；仅凭这句话，还不能说她没有想法，也不能说她喜欢被提醒。她也许早有同样的计划，也许正在学习动作。
在纸上画一个小箭头，标出木板从四到三再到五，比急着给人贴“会合作”或“不主动”的标签更有用。箭头留下的是可以核对的变化，标签却容易掩盖我们还不知道的部分。
我的感受，也是一条有范围的线索
假如你亲自玩这一局，等小雨决定时觉得着急，这个感受可以留下。还可以补上具体时刻：小兔已经在第一块踏脚石上，中央剩三块，你担心下一轮没有木板。这样，“着急”就和一个局面连在一起了。
但你的着急不能代替小雨的感受。她可能觉得终于看懂了计划，正在兴奋地计算；也可能因为不知道收集会不会结束回合而犹豫。同样的停顿，可能来自认真比较，也可能来自规则疑问。观察到她停下来，与知道她为什么停下来，是两步不同的工作。
可以问“刚才轮到你时，你在考虑什么？”再把她的回答和动作放在一起看。若抢先问“是不是规则太难了？”，问题里已经塞进了设计者的猜测。她即使同意，也未必说明这就是最初的原因。
从一件小事，得到下一步问题
观察不必把桌上的每句话都抄下来。想看两人怎样决定谁留下，就留意提出计划、回应计划和实际行动的时点；想看木板是否容易分清，就留意纸片被拿起、放下和询问的地方。关注点帮我们选择要留下什么，却不能让不合预期的事情消失。如果两人根本没看懂轮到谁，这件事会影响之后的合作，也应该记住。
这一轮之后，比较稳妥的问题是：“玩家能否看出，留在起点也会帮助共同目标？”直接得出“应该让收集也前进一步”，则过早跳到了改法。这个改法还会取消留下来的代价，改变整个过河安排。
从动作、自己的感受和对原因的猜想中分清哪些已经知道，我们就能带着更具体的问题继续。接下来还要认识坐在桌边的人：同样的规则，在什么时间、什么地方，由什么样的玩家来玩，才是我们想设计的那一局？
What Have You Actually Seen After Watching a Game?

In the first round, Lin moves Rabbit forward one step. The shared supply drops from four planks to three. Yu then keeps Hedgehog on the starting bank and collects two new planks, bringing the supply to five. One animal has moved ahead; the other has stayed still. If we watch positions alone, Lin seems to be making progress while Yu holds things up.

But collecting changes the situation too. The animals need six moves between them, and their starting four planks cannot pay for all six. If both move in the first round, the two remaining planks cannot cover the four moves still needed. Both animals have also left the only place where they can collect. Watching positions and planks together reveals how staying still can help them cross.
A designer needs to notice the whole change. Otherwise, “the animal did not move” can become “that turn did nothing,” followed by a new action the game never needed.
Describe what happened before judging it

“They worked well together” already includes a judgment. “After Lin moved, three planks remained; Yu collected, bringing the supply to five” lets someone else reconstruct the situation. We can then add what people said, what they did first, and what happened next. Order matters: did Yu collect after a reminder from Lin, or did she suggest staying behind? Both paths can produce five planks while raising different questions.

These are two imagined possibilities, not reports of a real playtest. Suppose Lin says, “Stay there and collect first,” and Yu does. We can say that he proposed a plan and she followed it. That sentence alone cannot tell us whether she had ideas of her own or enjoyed the reminder. She may already have had the same plan, or she may still be learning the actions.

A little arrow showing the supply changing from four to three to five is more useful than quickly calling someone “cooperative” or “passive.” The arrow preserves a change we can check. The label can hide what we still do not know.
Your feelings are clues with limits

If you play this round and feel impatient while Yu decides, you can keep that observation too. Add the moment: Rabbit was on the first stepping stone, three planks remained, and you were worried about having enough next round. Now the feeling is connected to a particular situation.

Your impatience cannot tell us how Yu felt. She might be excited because she has just understood the plan. Or she might be unsure whether collecting ends her turn. The same pause could come from comparing choices or from a question about the rules. Seeing her pause and knowing why she paused are separate steps.

You could ask, “What were you considering when it was your turn?” and compare her answer with her actions. Asking “Were the rules too difficult?” puts the designer’s guess inside the question. Even if she agrees, that may not have been the original cause.
Turn a small event into a useful question

Observing does not require writing down every word. To understand how players decide who stays behind, watch when they propose plans, respond, and act. To understand whether the planks are easy to distinguish, watch where pieces are picked up and placed, and where questions arise. A focus helps us choose what to record. It should still leave room for surprises. If neither player knows whose turn it is, that will affect their cooperation too.

After this round, a useful question is: “Can players recognize that staying on the starting bank can help their shared goal?” Jumping straight to “collecting should also move the animal forward” skips ahead to a change. That change would remove the cost of staying behind and alter how the crossing works.

Separating actions, your own feelings, and guesses about causes gives us a clearer question to carry forward. Next we need to consider the people at the table: who will play, where, and when? Those conditions help define the game we are trying to make.
这款游戏给谁，在什么时候玩？
设想小林把小动物过河带到活动室。小雨愿意一起看看，但十分钟后要去上课。两人身边只有一张小桌子，桌上还放着书包。这和周末有整张桌子、可以慢慢商量的下午，是两种不同的开始。
同一套规则没有改变，能用来听说明、摆材料和考虑下一步的条件却变了。设计游戏时，“给新手玩”还不够具体。我们需要知道，新手将在什么情况下遇见它。
年龄没有替我们回答的问题
同样十二岁的两个人，一个可能已经熟悉轮流行动，另一个第一次听见“每人一次才算一轮”。前者未必喜欢竞争，后者也未必只想玩简单的游戏。年龄可以提醒我们检查用词，却不能替代这些具体了解。
回到这次假设的活动室相遇，小林可以先说：“这是两个人一起想办法过河的游戏。你愿意看一轮，再决定要不要接着玩吗？”小雨知道自己将做什么，也知道现在的答应没有包下整个下午。若她只想观看，小林可以演示两只动物的一轮，不把旁观误算成她已加入游戏。
介绍还可以消除一种不必要的疑惑。假如小雨问：“小兔先到了，是我输了吗？”答案是，两只都到岸才一起获胜，没有个人名次。这个问题暴露的是她带来的理解方式。把目标说清，比从这个问题判断她“不会玩”更有用。
时间要装下游戏之外的事
基本版最多四轮，但四轮不是四分钟。第一次读动作、数木板、商量谁留在起点收集，都需要时间；玩完还要收拾。没有实际计时，就不能向小雨保证十分钟一定够。
有几种不同的处理办法。今天只演示第一轮，目标是看懂一次行动；两人另约一段更充裕的时间，目标是完成一局；或者先尝试完整游戏，到了上课时间就停下。前两种改变这次活动的安排，第三种需要事先知道如何停。
如果铃声响了而两只动物还没到岸，可以把这次记录为“中途停止”，然后收好材料。基本规则的失败发生在第四轮结束仍未到齐；上课打断不是动物又做了一个动作，也不用把自愿参与变成必须熬完的承诺。
桌面同样要具体看。两只动物、一条路线、中央可用木板、旁边已用木板以及桌外备用纸片，需要各自找得到的地方。桌子太挤，可以先挪开书包或换位置。是否看得清、够得着，后面还会仔细讨论；现在先发现游戏依赖哪些条件。
让人谈什么，比让人说多少更重要
假如这次见面的愿望是两人一起商量，值得保留的可能是：“谁这次留在起点，好让另一只先走？”若他们一边聊天一边玩，每一步又要读一长段新文字，规则阅读就会和聊天争用注意。多加故事或选择，未必更符合这次见面的愿望。
另一桌的人可能恰好想安静计算。有明确的路线和有限木板，就有东西可想。小林不能因为对方话少，便认定需要增加抢答；也不能因为一个人很兴奋，就认定另一个人同样享受。这些判断需要当事人的话和具体发生的事来修正。
起点是可以改的判断
现在我们能给这次设计一个比“适合十二岁”更清楚的起点：“两位第一次接触它的朋友，在能坐下摆材料的地方，愿意用一段不赶时间的空闲，共同商量一个短小问题。”这里的每一项都有用处：两人限制人数，初次接触要求说明够清楚，共同商量给动作之间的关系一个方向。
这些条件可以随着了解改变。若朋友总是错开时间，可能要设计能保存局面和轮次的另一种玩法；若大家其实只想看一段演示，也可以把这次活动做成可停下观看的介绍。条件变了，设计方向可以跟着改，无须先责怪玩家没照原计划出现。
有了这样一个暂定场景，下一章就能再往前一步：这次设计最想让人做什么，先做多大，还有什么必须留待验证。
Who Will Play This Game, and When?

Imagine Lin bringing the animal crossing game to an activity room. Yu would like to see it, but she has a class in ten minutes. They have a small table with schoolbags already on it. This is a different starting point from a weekend afternoon with a whole table and time to talk.

The rules are the same. The conditions for hearing an explanation, setting out pieces, and considering a move have changed. “For beginners” is not yet specific enough for a design. We need to know how those beginners will encounter it.
Questions an age cannot answer

Two twelve-year-olds may bring different experience. One already understands taking turns; the other first encounters the idea that both players must act to complete a round. The experienced player may dislike competition, while the newcomer may want a substantial challenge. Age can prompt us to check our wording. It cannot answer these more specific questions.

In our imagined meeting, Lin could say, “This is a game about finding a way across together. Would you like to see one round, then decide whether to continue?” Yu can understand both the activity and the extent of her agreement. If she prefers to watch, Lin can demonstrate a round for both animals without treating her presence as a commitment to play.

An introduction can also resolve an unnecessary uncertainty. Suppose Yu asks, “If Rabbit arrives first, have I lost?” Both animals must arrive for a shared win; there are no individual places. Her question reveals an expectation she brought with her. Explaining the goal is more useful than deciding that she is bad at games.
Time must hold more than the turns

The basic game lasts at most four rounds, but four rounds do not mean four minutes. Reading the actions, counting planks, and discussing who will stay at the start to collect all take time. Packing up does too. Without timing an actual session, we cannot promise that ten minutes will be enough.

Different arrangements serve different purposes. Today they could demonstrate just the first round to understand an action. They could arrange more time to finish a game. Or they could attempt a whole game and stop when class begins. The first two change the plan for this meeting. The third needs an understood way to stop.

If the bell rings before both animals arrive, they can record the session as “stopped partway” and pack up. Under the basic rules, a loss occurs when the fourth round ends without both animals across. A class interrupting the session is not another animal action, and agreeing to try a game need not become an obligation to finish it.

Space also needs a concrete look. The animals, route, available planks in the center, used planks beside them, and reserve paper pieces off the table need identifiable places. Moving the bags or changing tables may help. Later we will examine seeing and reaching the pieces more closely. For now, we are noticing conditions the game depends on.
What people discuss matters more than how much they speak

Suppose the purpose of this meeting is to think together. A question worth preserving might be, “Who stays at the start this time so the other animal can move?” If they want to chat while playing, a long new passage to read on every turn would compete with that conversation. More story or more choices may not serve this particular meeting.

Another pair may want quiet calculation. A clear route and a limited supply of planks give them something to consider. Quiet players do not automatically need a speed contest added, and one person’s excitement does not establish the other person’s enjoyment. Their accounts and specific events can help revise our assumptions.
A starting judgment can change

We can now describe a more useful starting point than “suitable for twelve-year-olds”: “Two friends meeting this game for the first time, somewhere they can sit and lay out pieces, with an unhurried stretch of free time to discuss a small shared problem.” Each part does work. Two people sets a player count. First contact calls for a clear explanation. Shared discussion gives a direction to the relationships between actions.

These conditions can change as we learn. If the friends can never arrive together, a different design might preserve the position and turns between visits. If people mainly want to watch a demonstration, the meeting could become an introduction they can leave when they wish. A changed situation can justify a changed direction without blaming people for failing to appear as expected.
This provisional setting gives the next chapter a starting point: what do we want people to do, how much should we build first, and what still needs checking?
还没有规则时，先确定什么？
“我们来做一个小动物过河游戏。”听起来已经有了方向，两位设计者却可能在想完全不同的事。一位想让动物争着先到岸，另一位想让它们一起想办法。河、木板和可爱的角色可以完全相同，玩家要关心的事却不同。
先把这处分歧说清，比马上决定木板画多大更有帮助。争先过河时，阻碍对方也许很有用；共同过河时，让同伴留下准备材料也许是在帮助整个队伍。目的没有说清，之后每增加一条规则，都可能把游戏拉向不同方向。
先描述想让人遇到的处境
我们已经见过完整的过河基本版。现在试着倒过来，想象规则尚未确定时，怎样为它写一个暂定方向：两个人坐在一张小桌边，玩一局能在短暂空闲里结束的纸片游戏。他们需要商量各自什么时候前进、什么时候为共同目标做准备；希望每个人都有自己的决定，而双方都到岸才算完成。
这几句话可以成为一份很短的设计简报。它说明为谁、在什么条件下做、希望发生什么，也留下尚未确定的地方。此时不必知道一定用四轮、四块木板，或一定收集两块。那些是之后可以比较的规则方案。
“希望两人商量”也还不是已经实现的结果。一人可能想好全部安排，另一人只照做。所以还可以留下一个要观察的问题：两个人是否都有机会提出和选择自己的行动？写下目标，是为了让后来的草稿有一个可检查的方向。
哪些事情固定，哪些事情还能换？
假设这次只能使用纸和笔，桌面也不大，这是制作条件。它会让长长的立体河道不太合适，却不自动决定玩家应当合作还是竞争。“双方都到岸才算完成”则是当前选择的体验方向。为了实现它，可以尝试共用木板，也可以先构思别的互相帮助方式。
把条件和方向分开，我们就知道该怎样回应新点子。“加一个会发光的电子桥”可能超出这次能做的材料；“第一个到岸的人单独获胜”则改变了谁在乎谁能过河。两者都不是单纯的好坏问题，而是在改变简报中的不同部分。
有些限制只是为了先做出一小段可玩的东西。我们可以暂时只画一条路线，先看两人怎样分配准备与前进。等这个关系清楚后，再判断第二条路线是否有帮助。暂时没做，不等于永远禁止。
简报怎样帮助选择，又不把人困住？
假如桌上有两个候选点子：让动物换三种帽子，或者让留在起点的动物为双方取得木板。前者也许有趣，但在目前的方向下，后者更直接地让“一人的准备影响两人的行程”出现。这个理由足够让我们先试收集，不需要宣布帽子永远没有价值。
简报也可能需要改变。如果之后发现自己更想做轻松的角色装扮游戏，就可以承认方向变了，再重新考虑规则。问题在于改了方向却还用旧目标评价每个点子：一边要求紧张规划，一边不断消除所有需要规划的限制，改稿便会互相抵消。
目前这份简报还不能保证有人喜欢游戏，也不能代替完整规则。它完成的是更早的一件事：把模糊的“做个好玩的游戏”变成一个可以讨论的意图。接下来，我们就能围绕这个意图多想几种做法，再挑一种写成真正可以执行的动作。
What Can You Decide Before You Have Rules?

“Let’s make a game about animals crossing a river.” That sounds like a direction, yet two designers may picture very different games. One imagines animals racing to arrive first. The other imagines them working things out together. The river, planks, and cute characters could look identical while giving players different things to care about.

Clearing up that difference helps more than immediately deciding how large to draw a plank. In a race, getting in someone’s way might be useful. In a shared crossing, staying behind to prepare materials might help the whole team. Without a clear purpose, each added rule could pull the game in a different direction.
Describe the situation you want players to face

We have already seen the complete base crossing game. Now imagine working backward to a time when its rules were undecided. A provisional direction might be: two people at a small table play a paper game that fits into a short break. They discuss when each should move and when someone should prepare for their shared goal. Each person should have decisions of their own, and the task is complete only when both animals arrive.

Those few sentences can serve as a short design brief. They say who the game is for, the conditions it must fit, and what we hope will happen. They also leave things open. We do not yet need to choose four rounds, four starting planks, or collecting two planks at a time. Those are rule proposals to compare later.

“We hope they will discuss their plans” is not an achieved result. One person might decide everything while the other follows. So we can keep a question for observation: does each person have opportunities to propose and choose their own actions? Writing down a goal gives later drafts something to check.
What is fixed, and what can change?

Suppose we only have paper and pens, and our table is small. Those are practical conditions. They make a long, three-dimensional river awkward, but do not decide whether players should cooperate or compete. “Both animals must arrive” is the direction we have currently chosen. Shared planks are one possible way to support it; other ways of helping each other could be explored too.

Keeping conditions separate from direction helps us respond to ideas. An electronic bridge that lights up may exceed our available materials. Giving victory only to the first arrival changes whose crossing matters to whom. These proposals affect different parts of the brief, so simply calling either one “good” or “bad” misses the decision involved.

Some limits are temporary ways to get a small piece working. We can start with one route to see how players divide preparation and movement. Once that relationship is clear, we can decide whether a second route helps. Leaving something out for now does not ban it forever.
Use the brief to choose without getting trapped

Suppose we have two ideas: give each animal three hats to wear, or let an animal on the starting bank collect planks for both players. Hats might be enjoyable. But for our current direction, collecting more directly creates the relationship we want: one person’s preparation changes both animals’ journeys. That is a reason to try collecting first, without declaring hats worthless.

The brief can change too. If we later discover that we would rather make a relaxed character-dressing game, we can acknowledge the new direction and reconsider the rules. Trouble comes when the direction changes but we keep judging ideas against an old goal. Asking for tense planning while removing every reason to plan can make successive changes cancel each other out.

This brief cannot guarantee that anyone will enjoy the game, and it cannot replace complete rules. It does an earlier job: turning “make something fun” into an intention we can discuss. Next we can imagine several ways to serve that intention, then choose one to turn into an action people can actually carry out.
有了方向，怎样想出不止一种做法？
我们暂定要做一个两人合作过河的纸片游戏：每个人决定自己的动作，同时得顾及同伴。可是，“让玩家合作”还不能告诉我们轮到一个人时，他究竟能做什么。需要把方向往桌面上推近一点。
先想一个具体时刻。小兔到了第一块踏脚石，小刺猬还在岸上；接下来，小刺猬做什么，能影响小兔的处境？它可以取得供双方使用的木板，也可以传递某件东西，或在岸上操作一座桥。这些目前只是候选想法。传递给谁、桥怎样起作用，都还没写清，不能立刻混进基本版。
把同一时刻想成几种不同做法，可以防止我们把最先想到的答案当成唯一答案。随后还得看，每种做法究竟要求增加什么。
从已经知道的东西往外想
构思不一定从一个完整故事开始。手边有纸片，可以想“玩家怎样移动、翻转或分给别人”；已经有河流场景，可以想“过河前要准备什么”；希望两个人互相影响，可以想“一人做什么会改变另一人的选择”。这些入口能够通向同一个设计问题，无须先把整个世界的故事写完。
但只换场景名称，未必产生了新玩法。把“取得木板”叫作“采集魔法叶子”，如果取得条件、数量和用法都相同，玩家作决定时仍面对相同的关系。换名字可能帮助读者理解主题；若我们此刻要找另一种合作方式，就需要继续改变动作或后果。
也可以先把暂时不完整的点子留下。“一人留在岸上准备，另一人先走”已经指出一种互相影响的可能。现在不必立刻给它加天气、道具、角色能力和三种计分。把这些一起加上，会让我们难以看清最初的关系是否成立。
什么时候开始挑选？
产生想法时，过早追问每个细节，会让所有点子都因为“还没写完”而消失。反过来，一直增加点子也不会自动得到可玩的游戏。到了要做第一张纸的时候，就可以把候选放回暂定方向下比较。
以“收集共用木板”和“操作一座桥”为例。前者至少需要可用木板、花过的木板和取得新木板的条件。后者还需要说明桥何时打开、能让谁通过、会不会关闭，以及操作它的人能否离开。这些问题都有可能得到有趣的答案。眼前如果只想先看“谁留下准备”，收集方案已经能把这个关系摆出来，所需说明也更少，因此适合先试。
这不是说规则少的点子永远更好。若目标本来就是两人配合开关桥，桥的这些细节便是要探索的内容。合适的范围来自这次想弄清什么，而不只是数一数有几条规则。
留下一个候选，给它补上能执行的细节
我们于是先选择收集：留在岸上的动物取得木板，双方都能用。它直接连接了个人动作与共同进度。接下来必须追问：只有岸上能收集吗？取得几块？收集后还能移动吗？已经用掉的木板会不会回来？不同答案会形成不同游戏。
基本版选择的是：只在起点收集，每次取得两块新木板，收集用掉这一回合，不能再移动，花掉的木板不再使用。这些条件让留下准备有帮助，也有时间代价。如果可以无限地免费收集，先准备多少就不再是同一种问题。
其他点子仍可以留作后来比较的候选。它们不必偷偷成为下一章的额外规则。现在我们只带着已经选中的关系继续：怎样把“收集”和“前进”写成别人能准确做出来的动作，让纸上的小动物真的开始过河？
How Can One Direction Lead to Several Ideas?

Our provisional direction is a paper game in which two people cooperate to cross a river. Each controls their own actions while considering their partner. But “make players cooperate” does not tell us what someone can actually do on a turn. We need to bring that direction closer to the table.

Start with a particular moment. Rabbit is on the first stepping stone; Hedgehog is still on the bank. What could Hedgehog do that would affect Rabbit’s situation? Hedgehog might obtain planks both animals can use, pass something along, or operate a bridge from the bank. These are only candidate ideas. We have not decided who can receive an item or how the bridge works, so none of them should silently enter the base game.
Imagining several actions for the same moment helps us avoid treating our first answer as the only answer. Then we can examine what each proposal would require.
Expand from something you already have

An idea does not have to begin with a complete story. With paper pieces in hand, we can ask how players might move, turn over, or share them. With a river setting, we can ask what needs preparing before a crossing. If we want two people to affect each other, we can ask what one person could do to change the other’s choices. These starting points can lead toward the same design problem without requiring a whole fictional world first.

Changing names alone may leave the play unchanged. If “collecting planks” becomes “gathering magical leaves,” but the conditions, quantities, and uses stay the same, players still face the same decisions. A new name may help communicate the theme. To find a different way of cooperating, we need to change an action or its consequences too.

We can also keep an idea before every detail is settled. “One animal prepares on the bank while the other moves ahead” already suggests a useful relationship. It does not immediately need weather, items, special powers, and three kinds of scoring. Adding all those things at once would make the original relationship harder to examine.
When should you start choosing?

During idea generation, demanding every detail too early can eliminate everything for being unfinished. Yet collecting more ideas indefinitely will not produce a playable game either. When we are ready to make the first paper draft, we can compare candidates against our provisional direction.

Consider shared plank collection and operating a bridge. Collection needs available planks, spent planks, and conditions for obtaining new ones. A bridge needs rules for when it opens, who can cross, whether it closes again, and whether the operator can leave. Those questions might have interesting answers. If our immediate question is simply “who stays behind to prepare?”, collecting already makes that relationship visible with fewer things to explain. That makes it a useful first candidate.

Fewer rules are not always better. If our goal were coordinating a bridge’s opening and closing, those details would be the very things we needed to explore. The useful scope depends on the question, not merely the number of rules.
Give the chosen idea details people can carry out

So we start with collecting: an animal on the bank obtains planks that either animal can use. This directly connects an individual action to shared progress. Now we must ask: can animals collect only on the bank? How many planks do they get? Can they move afterward? Do spent planks return? Different answers create different games.

The base game chooses these answers: collect only on the starting bank, obtain two new planks, use the whole turn to collect, and never reuse spent planks. These conditions make preparation helpful while giving it a cost in time. Unlimited free collection would create a different planning problem.

The other ideas can remain candidates for later comparison. They do not have to become extra rules in the next chapter. For now, we carry forward one relationship: how can we write collecting and moving so precisely that another person can perform them and the paper animals can begin their crossing?
“让动物过河”，要变成哪些动作？
“帮助小动物过河”说明了我们希望完成什么，还没有说明玩家怎样做。拿起小兔放到对岸，也算把它送过河，却绕开了整个游戏。设计动作，要把故事里的愿望变成桌上允许发生的变化。
我们先做一份可以直接运行的基本版纸上草稿，再看看每个动作为什么要写这些细节。它只需要画线、写字和移动纸片，外观可以在规则清楚以后继续修改。
把一局需要的东西摆出来
纸上画四个位置，依次连接：起点河岸、第一块踏脚石、第二块踏脚石、对岸。另做小兔和小刺猬两张动物纸片、二十张木板纸片，以及一个用来指示第几轮的标记。写出“第1轮”到“第4轮”，把标记放在第1轮。再写一个先指向小林的回合提示，避免忘记轮到谁。
小林控制小兔，小雨控制小刺猬，两只都放在起点。二十张木板中，四张放在中央的“可用木板”区，十六张放在另一个“备用纸片”区；旁边再留出空的“已用木板”区。备用纸片表示还没取得的新木板，和已经花过的木板分开。
最多玩四轮，每轮先小林、后小雨，每人各一个回合。轮到自己时，从下面三种动作中选一种：
前进：中央至少有一块可用木板时，花一块，把自己的动物向对岸移动到下一个相邻位置。不能后退或跳过位置。花掉的木板放入已用区，之后不再使用。
收集：自己的动物还在起点时，从备用区取两张新木板放到中央。动物留在原位，这个回合不能再前进。
等待：动物和木板都不改变，结束自己的回合。
两只动物可以停在同一位置，不互相阻挡。已经到对岸的动物，后面的回合只能等待。玩家可以讨论，但各自决定自己动物的动作。只要双方都到对岸，立刻共同获胜；第四轮双方都行动后，若还没一起到岸，就共同失败。没有个人分数，也没有天气或额外能力。
四轮最多有八次收集，十六张备用纸片足以表示这些新木板。备用区是让我们能够摆出局面的材料供给，不是玩家开始就拥有的木板。把它们全放进中央，就已经改了游戏。
动作里，什么最需要写清？
第一轮小林选择前进：先确认中央有木板，拿出一块放进已用区，再把小兔放到第一块踏脚石。中央从四块变三块，小林的回合结束。小雨选择收集，就从备用区取两块放到中央，让三块变成五块，小刺猬仍在起点。
“前进”和“收集”之所以能执行，是因为我们写清了谁可以做、什么时候可以做、要付出什么，以及完成后改变什么。若只写“前进花木板”，别人仍不知道花几块、走几格、是否能跳过小兔，也不知道木板花到哪里。动作名称再形象，也不能替这些缺口作决定。
有些决定则需要看更长的过程。收集不移动动物，却可能为之后的前进提供缺少的木板；它用掉一个回合，也可能让留下的动物来不及到岸。这个动作的作用来自它和整段过河的关系。我们无需要求每次拿两张纸片本身都惊险，才承认它对游戏有用。
哪些是选择，哪些是照规则处理？
小林选择前进，是在决定要做什么。把花掉的木板放进已用区，是在执行这个决定应有的结果；他不能顺手选择把木板留在中央。两件事都由手完成，却承担不同作用。
在桌游里，玩家还替游戏维护位置、资源和轮次。若这些更新漏了一项，下一位玩家面对的就可能是错误局面。下一章会把一次动作从开始到结束慢慢走完：先检查什么，什么时候付款、移动、换人，又在哪一刻判断这一局已经结束。
What Actions Turn “Help the Animals Cross” into a Game?

“Help the animals cross the river” tells us what we want to accomplish, but not how players do it. Picking up Rabbit and placing him on the far bank would complete the crossing while skipping the game. Designing actions means turning a story’s intention into changes that are allowed on the table.

We will first make a paper draft of the complete base game, then examine why its actions need these details. Drawing lines, writing labels, and moving pieces are enough to start. Its appearance can change as the rules become clearer.
Put the pieces of a whole game on the table

Draw four connected spaces in order: the starting bank, the first stepping stone, the second stepping stone, and the far bank. Make a Rabbit piece, a Hedgehog piece, twenty paper planks, and a round marker. Write rounds 1 to 4 and place the marker on round 1. Add a turn reminder pointing first to Lin so that players can keep track of whose turn it is.

Lin controls Rabbit; Yu controls Hedgehog. Both animals start on the starting bank. Put four planks in a central area labeled “Available planks,” and sixteen in a separate area labeled “Spare pieces.” Leave an empty area labeled “Spent planks.” Spare pieces represent new planks that have not been collected. Keep them separate from planks that have already been spent.
Play for up to four rounds. In each round, Lin takes one turn, then Yu takes one turn. On your turn, choose one of these three actions:

Move: If at least one available plank remains, spend one and move your animal to the next adjacent space toward the far bank. You cannot move backward or skip a space. Put the plank in the spent area; it cannot be used again.

Collect: If your animal is still on the starting bank, take two new planks from the spare area and add them to the shared available supply. Your animal stays where it is. You cannot also move this turn.
Wait: Leave animals and planks unchanged and end your turn.

Animals may share a space and do not block each other. An animal on the far bank can only wait on later turns. Players may discuss their plans, but each decides their own animal’s action. As soon as both animals reach the far bank, the players win together. If they have not both arrived after both turns of round 4, they lose together. There are no personal scores, weather, or special abilities.

Four rounds allow at most eight collect actions, so sixteen spare pieces can represent all the new planks those actions could produce. The spare area supplies pieces for representing the game; it is not a stock the players already own. Putting all twenty planks in the center would change the game.
Which details does an action need?

In round 1, Lin chooses to move. He checks that an available plank remains, puts one in the spent area, and moves Rabbit to the first stepping stone. The shared supply falls from four to three, and his turn ends. If Yu collects, she takes two planks from the spare area and adds them to the center, raising the supply to five. Hedgehog stays on the starting bank.

These actions work because we have specified who can perform them, when they are allowed, what they cost, and what changes afterward. “Movement costs planks” leaves too much unanswered: how many planks, how far, whether an animal can skip past Rabbit, and where the spent pieces go. A vivid action name cannot fill those gaps.

An action’s role may also depend on the longer journey. Collecting moves no animal, but can supply planks needed for later moves. It uses a turn and may leave the collecting animal too little time to arrive. Its value comes from its relationship with the crossing. Picking up two paper pieces does not have to feel thrilling on its own for the action to matter.
What is a choice, and what carries it out?

When Lin chooses to move, he decides what to do. Putting the plank in the spent area carries out the required consequence. He cannot also choose to leave that plank available. Both involve his hands, but they serve different purposes.

In a tabletop game, players also maintain positions, resources, and the round. Missing an update can give the next player an incorrect situation. The next chapter follows a whole action carefully: what to check first, when to pay and move, when to change players, and exactly when to decide that the game has ended.
一个动作结束以后，桌上应该变成什么样？
小林已经把小兔移到第一块踏脚石，却忘了花掉中央的一块木板。现在纸上显示四块可用木板，正确数量却应当是三块。小雨再认真计算，也是在错误的起点上计算。
可玩的动作需要两部分配合：玩家知道自己能选什么，大家也知道选完后怎样得到下一个正确局面。这一章仍用上一章那份完整纸片草稿：两只动物、四个位置、中央四块可用木板、十六块备用纸片，以及空的已用区；每轮先小林后小雨，最多四轮。这里没有增加新规则，只把执行过程看得更细。
先确认允许，再一起完成变化
轮到小林时，他先确认小兔在哪里。如果已经在对岸，就只能等待；如果还在途中，中央至少有一块可用木板时才能前进。决定前进后，把一块可用木板放入已用区，并把小兔向对岸移到相邻位置。这两件事合在一起，才算完成这个动作。
若中央没有木板，小林不能先移动，再留下“下次补付”的欠账。基本版没有借木板规则。他需要选择当前允许的其他动作：仍在起点可以收集，已经离开起点就只能等待。这样，下一位玩家不必猜动物的位置是否还在等一次付款。
收集也有明确的完成状态。动物必须在起点，从备用区取两张新木板放进中央，动物不动，随后结束回合。拿回已用区的木板会改变“花掉便不再使用”的规则。三个区摆得分明，能帮助大家把同样形状的纸片用对。
我们可以把这些此刻有效的信息叫作游戏的“状态”：动物在哪、中央还剩多少、谁行动、到了第几轮。用过和备用的纸片放在哪里，也帮助我们正确维护它。状态不只是棋子所在的那一格。
等待没有移动，也要把回合交出去
假设第一轮小林前进，小雨收集。小林做完后，可用木板是三块，小兔在第一块踏脚石，提示转向小雨；轮次仍是第一轮。小雨做完后，可用木板是五块，小刺猬仍在起点。两人这才都行动过，可以把轮标移到第二轮，再把回合提示转回小林。
等待时，动物和木板都不改变，回合却仍然结束。否则，一位玩家可以说自己一直在等待，而另一位永远轮不到。已经到岸的动物也是如此：它在以后的回合等待，然后把行动机会交给同伴。
纸片和标记让这种更新能被看见。将来若用程序代替人移动轮标，谁先谁后、何时换轮的规则仍然需要写清。自动执行可以省去手工，却不能替设计者决定漏掉的步骤。
最后一次行动，先看成功还是先看期限？
看一条能完成过河的安排：第一轮小兔前进、小刺猬收集；第二轮双方前进；第三轮双方前进，此时小兔到岸、小刺猬在第二块踏脚石，中央剩一块；第四轮小兔等待，小刺猬花最后一块前进。
这时双方到岸，应当立即共同获胜。虽然第四轮也刚好用完，期限不能把刚完成的成功盖掉。因此，每个动作完成后先看双方是否都到岸；没有成功，才在第四轮双方都行动完时判定失败。第二轮或第三轮还没到岸，也不能提早因为“仍有人没到”而宣布失败。
这个顺序是规则的一部分。它避免同一局面因为不同人先想起不同句子，得到相反结果。写清后，可以从第一轮一路手动走到结束，看看每个时刻是否都有下一步。
我们现在有了一份能运行并判定结束的草稿。接下来可以追问更有意思的问题：当玩家面前有两个允许的动作时，它们是否真的值得比较，还是其中一个永远没有理由被选？
What Should the Table Look Like After an Action?

Lin has moved Rabbit to the first stepping stone but forgotten to spend a plank. The table still shows four available planks when there should be three. However carefully Yu now plans, she will be planning from the wrong starting point.

A playable action needs two things to work together: players know what they may choose, and everyone knows how to produce the correct situation afterward. We are using the complete paper draft from the previous chapter: two animals, four spaces, four available planks, sixteen spare pieces, and an empty spent area. Lin goes before Yu in each round, for up to four rounds. We are adding no rules here, only examining how to carry them out.
Check permission, then complete the changes

On Lin’s turn, he first checks Rabbit’s position. On the far bank, Rabbit can only wait. Elsewhere on the route, he can move if at least one available plank remains. After choosing to move, Lin puts one available plank in the spent area and moves Rabbit to the next adjacent space toward the far bank. Together, these changes complete the action.

With no available planks, Lin cannot move now and promise to pay later. The base game has no borrowing rule. He must choose another action currently allowed: collect if Rabbit is still on the starting bank, or wait if Rabbit has left it. The next player should not have to guess whether an animal’s position is waiting for a payment.

Collecting also has a definite result. The animal must be on the starting bank. Take two new planks from the spare area, add them to the center, leave the animal where it is, and end the turn. Taking pieces from the spent area would change the rule that spent planks cannot be reused. Three distinct areas help players handle pieces that otherwise look the same.

The information that currently matters—animal positions, available planks, whose turn it is, and the round—is the game’s “state.” Keeping spare and spent pieces in their proper places helps maintain it. State includes more than the space a piece occupies.
Waiting still passes the turn

Suppose Rabbit moves and Hedgehog collects in round 1. After Lin’s action, three planks remain, Rabbit is on the first stepping stone, and the turn reminder points to Yu. It is still round 1. After Yu’s action, five planks are available and Hedgehog remains on the starting bank. Only now have both players acted. Move the round marker to round 2 and the turn reminder back to Lin.

Waiting leaves animals and planks unchanged, but it still ends the turn. Otherwise, someone could claim to be waiting indefinitely while their partner never gets a turn. The same applies to an animal that has already arrived: it waits on later turns, then passes the opportunity to act to its partner.

Pieces and markers make these updates visible. If a program eventually moves the round marker for us, we must still specify turn order and when a round changes. Automation can replace manual work; it cannot decide a missing rule for the designer.
At the deadline, do we check success or failure first?

Consider this successful plan. In round 1, Rabbit moves and Hedgehog collects. Both move in round 2 and again in round 3. Rabbit has now arrived, Hedgehog is on the second stepping stone, and one plank remains. In round 4, Rabbit waits and Hedgehog spends the last plank to move.

Both animals have arrived, so the players win immediately. Round 4 has also just ended, but reaching the deadline must not erase the success just completed. After each action, first check whether both animals have arrived. If they have not, check for failure only after both turns of round 4. Not having both animals across in round 2 or 3 is not yet a reason to declare failure.

This order belongs in the rules. It prevents the same situation producing opposite results because different people remember different sentences first. Once the order is clear, we can walk the draft from round 1 to the finish and check that each moment has a next step.

We now have a draft that can run and reach a definite ending. Next comes another question: when players have two permitted actions, are both worth considering, or is there never a reason to choose one of them?
轮到我时，为什么要想一想？
前面我们已经把一次行动拆成决定、付费和更新局面。现在回到基本版的第一轮：小兔先走上了踏脚石，小刺猬却留在岸边收集木板。小雨并没有直接追上朋友。她做的这一步，最后让两只动物都有材料过河。
我们把时间退回她决定之前：小兔在第一块石头，小刺猬还在起点，中央剩三块木板。现在轮到小雨。她可以前进，也可以收集，还可以等待。要理解她为什么可能停下来想一想，先把两种做法分别往后走。
跟着走，会留下什么？
如果小雨也花一块木板，小刺猬就会来到第一块石头，和小兔站在一起。中央剩两块。眼前看起来很顺利：两只都出发了，没有谁落在后面。
不过，每只动物还得再走两步才能到对岸。两只合起来，需要四块木板，中央却只有两块。更麻烦的是，收集只能在起点进行；现在两只都离开了那里，又不能退回去。它们缺的两块木板，已经没有办法补上。
下一轮还可以继续移动几步，但按这套规则，这条路线已经无法让两只都到岸。问题出在第一轮结束时失去了继续收集的机会，不能等木板真的用光才看见。
如果小雨改为收集，情况就不同。小刺猬暂时没走，中央却从三块变成五块。小兔还有两步，小刺猬还有三步，合起来正好需要五块。小刺猬剩下三轮，每轮前进一步，也赶得上。留在岸边的这一回合，让后面的路仍然走得通。
得到两块，也放弃了一步
收集当然有好处，但它占用了小雨这次前进的机会。规则只允许每回合做一件事，不能把木板拿到手，再补走一步。我们比较的因此不是“拿两块”和“什么也没有”，而是“拿两块并留在岸边”与“走一步并少一块”。
选择某件事时放弃的其他机会，常被叫作“机会成本”。这里没有给收集标上价格，小雨仍然付出了一个回合。她愿不愿意这样做，要看这个回合能换来什么。
同一个“收集”，也不能一直被当成好答案。假如小林开局先收集，中央就从四块变成六块，小兔还在起点。接着轮到小雨，她让小刺猬前进，中央剩五块。两只以后都还有足够的木板和行动机会，可以完成过河。这次先收集的是小林，小雨就能够放心先走。
所以，“前进不好，收集好”没有说明真正的区别。我们需要看谁还在岸边、中央有多少木板，以及谁还来得及把缺少的材料补上。动作的名字相同，所处的时刻不同，它帮助解决的问题也会不同。
看见选项，还要看懂它怎样改变以后
设想小雨说：“我以为到了石头上也能收集。”她仍然看见了前进和收集两个选择，却是在按另一条规则计划。即使把两个按钮画得更大，也没有解释为什么离岸会改变后续机会。
这时，一句具体提醒比“请认真想一想”更有帮助：“你走出去以后，就不能再收集了。”它指出了哪个结果需要纳入判断，最后做什么仍由小雨决定。她可以问问题，可以说明自己的计划，也可以接受朋友的建议。
若小林直接替她拿木板、移动小刺猬，小雨虽然还坐在桌边，决定的过程却被跳过去了。能用手移动一个棋子，与能够决定这一步，未必是同一件事。这种能够通过自己的决定改变后果的能力，可以叫“能动性”。在这里，把它放回刚才的对比，就很具体：我的决定，确实能让接下来发生的事不同。
这也不表示玩家必须独自解决所有问题。小雨主动问“我们还差几块”，仍然可以在听完回答后作决定。帮助她看懂后果，与替她选好答案，做的是不同工作。
如果设计者希望小雨看得懂这次选择，可以把“只在起点收集”放在收集动作旁，并让中央木板始终可见。这样，她能找到所需条件。若只是把正确动作画成醒目的箭头，她也许会照做，却没有看见为什么。要帮助她学会判断，就需要把离岸后失去的机会和剩余费用接起来。
算明白以后，还剩下什么？
这个过河例子很小。第一次看见“现在快一步，后来可能无路可走”的关系，值得想一想；当两人已经知道该怎样准备，再玩时可能很快就能决定。我们不用为保持困难而把数字写得更绕。
一个例子能够教清一件事，不代表它会一直带来新问题。若要继续发展成更耐玩的游戏，设计者还得思考下一次会有哪些不同的局面。下一章会沿着眼前的过河决定加入一种明确的变化：如果这次前进要花多少木板，要等天气揭晓才知道，玩家又能怎样安排？
Why Pause to Think on My Turn?

We have separated an action into deciding, paying, and updating the situation. Now return to the first round of the basic game: Rabbit moved onto a stepping stone while Hedgehog stayed on the bank to collect planks. Yu did not immediately follow her friend. Her action helped provide enough material for both animals to cross.

Return to the moment before she decides. Rabbit is on the first stone, Hedgehog is on the starting bank, and three planks remain. It is Yu's turn. She can move, collect, or wait. To understand why she might pause, let's follow two of those choices separately.
What Would Following Rabbit Leave Behind?
If Yu spends a plank to move Hedgehog, it joins Rabbit on the first stone. Two planks remain. Things seem to be going well: both animals have set out, and neither is behind.

Each animal, however, still needs two steps to reach the far bank. Together, they need four planks, but only two remain. Worse, collecting is allowed only on the starting bank. Both animals have left it, and neither can go backward. There is now no way to obtain the missing two planks.

They can still make a few more moves, but these rules no longer allow both to arrive. The problem begins when they lose the opportunity to collect at the end of the first round. We do not need to wait until the supply is empty to see it.

Suppose Yu collects instead. Hedgehog stays put, but the supply rises from three planks to five. Rabbit needs two more steps and Hedgehog needs three: exactly five planks altogether. Hedgehog has three rounds left, so moving once in each will also get it across in time. Staying behind for this turn keeps the later route possible.
Getting Two Planks Means Giving Up a Step

Collecting helps, but it uses Yu's opportunity to move this turn. Each turn allows one action. She cannot take the planks and then add a forward step. We are comparing “gain two and stay here” with “move forward and spend one,” rather than simply “gain two” with “gain nothing.”

The other opportunity you give up when choosing something is often called an opportunity cost. Collecting has no printed price, yet Yu still spends a turn on it. Whether that is worthwhile depends on what the turn makes possible.

Nor can collecting always be treated as the right answer. Suppose Lin collects at the start instead. The supply rises from four to six while Rabbit stays on the bank. Yu can then move Hedgehog, leaving five planks. Both animals still have enough planks and enough remaining turns to finish crossing. This time Lin prepared the supply, so Yu can set out.

“Moving is bad; collecting is good” therefore misses the important difference. We need to look at who remains on the bank, how many planks are available, and who can still obtain any that are missing. An action can have the same name while helping with a different problem at a different moment.
Seeing a Choice Includes Understanding What Follows

Imagine Yu saying, “I thought we could collect while on the stones, too.” She can see both available actions, but she is planning with a different rule in mind. Drawing bigger buttons would not explain why leaving the bank changes her future opportunities.

A specific reminder would help more than “Think carefully”: “Once you leave, you can't collect again.” It points out a consequence to consider while leaving the decision with Yu. She can ask questions, explain her plan, or accept advice.

If Lin simply takes a plank for her and moves Hedgehog himself, Yu remains at the table but misses the decision. Moving a piece with your hand and deciding its action are not necessarily the same thing. This ability to change consequences through your own decisions can be called agency. In the comparison we just followed, it has a concrete meaning: my decision can make what happens next different.

That does not require solving everything alone. Yu can ask, “How many more planks do we need?” and still decide after hearing the answer. Helping her understand the consequences and choosing the answer for her are different kinds of help.

To help Yu understand this choice, a designer can put “collect only on the starting bank” beside the collect action and keep the shared planks visible. She can then find the conditions she needs. A bright arrow pointing to the correct action might get her to follow it without understanding why. Helping her judge requires connecting the opportunity lost on departure with the costs still ahead.
What Remains Once We Understand?

This crossing example is small. The first discovery—that moving faster now can leave no way through later—can take some thought. Once both players understand how to prepare, they may decide quickly when they play again. We do not need to make the numbers harder to read just to preserve difficulty.

An example that explains one relationship does not necessarily keep producing new questions. To develop a game people want to revisit, a designer would need to consider what situations could differ next time. The next chapter follows the crossing decision through one explicit change: what if the number of planks needed for this move becomes known only when the weather is revealed?
早一点知道天气，我能改做什么？
前面的基本版里，木板数量、动物位置和每一步的费用都摆在面前。两人仍然需要想一想，因为眼前走得快，后来可能没有木板可用。现在我们再问一步：如果有件事还不知道，决定会怎样改变？
先想想小雨下一回合要做什么。她可能已经想好，只是还没告诉小林；也可能正在前进和收集之间犹豫。这两种“不知道”不一样。前一种可以通过询问得知，后一种还没有一个已经选好的答案。猜小雨会怎样选，也不能直接当成掷骰子的机会来算，因为她正在考虑两人的计划。
一张扣着的牌，藏住了什么？
我们给过河例子增加一次天气变化，只看一个动物的一次行动。为方便比较，另设一个局部情境：小刺猬仍在起点岸，中央只有一块木板。这一段只比较它这次能做什么，不追算整局胜负。
准备六张天气牌，四张晴天、两张雨天。把它们充分洗匀，抽出一张，面朝下放好。仅在这次行动中，晴天前进一步花一块木板，雨天则要两块。木板不足就不能前进。
这张已经抽出的牌有一个确定的图案，小林和小雨却都还没看见。翻开会让他们知道图案，并不是翻开的动作把晴天变成了雨天。如果改为他们决定以后才洗牌、抽牌，产生结果的步骤也变了；这里先保持抽法相同，只改变何时让玩家看见。
六张牌中四张能让这一块木板够用，另两张不能。充分洗匀后，抽中晴天的机会是六份中的四份，这就是这里的概率。它描述可能出现的结果，不是保证这次一定抽到什么。
先说“我要走”，再看天气
第一种安排里，小雨先决定这回合做什么，之后才能翻牌。假设她选择前进。
翻到晴天，她就用掉中央的一块木板，让小刺猬走上第一块石头。翻到雨天，需要两块，桌上却只有一块。这次前进便落空：小刺猬留在岸边，木板仍是一块，但本回合已经用掉，不能改为收集。
规则必须说清最后这句话。否则，有人会觉得“没走成就不算行动”，有人会觉得“选过就算”，两人其实在用不同的玩法。
小雨当然也可以一开始就选择收集，留在岸边，把木板增加到三块。我们刚才跟着看的，是她选择冒险前进之后会发生什么；不知道天气，并没有逼她必须冒险。
先看天气，再决定做什么
第二种安排只把翻牌提前。小雨看见晴天后，可以选择前进，花一块，走到第一块石头；看见雨天后，可以改为收集，留在岸边，把中央增加到三块。
天气牌没有变，走一步的费用没有变。雨天也仍然阻止她用一块木板前进。改变的是：她还没把这个回合交给某个动作，所以可以根据天气换一种做法。
把两种安排放到同一个雨天里看，差别更清楚。先承诺前进，小刺猬原地不动，仍有一块木板；先知道下雨再选择收集，小刺猬也没动，却有了三块。站在同一个地方，不代表这一回合留下了相同结果。
这里的“早知道有用”，来自一项具体机会：小刺猬还在岸边，能够收集。如果它已经在石头上，同样只剩一块木板，雨天时既不能前进，又不能收集。提早知道后选择等待，与先选前进却落空，可能留下相同的局面。更多消息要配合可用的行动，才让玩家有东西可以改变。
没看懂规则，是另一个问题
假设牌已经翻开，大家都看见雨天，小雨却以为仍只要一块木板。她缺少的不是天气消息，而是对费用规则的理解。再翻一张牌不会解决这件事，需要先把“雨天要两块”讲清楚。
因此，听见一句“我根本不知道怎么办”，可以顺着这一步问：是某件事已经发生但没看见，是别人还没作决定，还是眼前的说明没读懂？找到缺在哪里，才知道该提前揭晓、留下回应机会，或改写说明。
如果想从相同条件再次比较，先把天气牌放回，重新洗匀，再抽一张；不放回的话，牌堆里剩下的晴雨数量已经变化，机会也可能不同。我们不能一边改变抽法，一边仍把它当成刚才的六张牌。
例如，刚抽走一张晴天牌而不放回，余下五张就是三晴、两雨，下次晴天的机会变成五份中的三份。把抽走的牌一直朝上放着，大家随时能核对；把它扣起来，则可能要求大家记住刚才看过什么。抽法没有因此改变，改变的是记住和查找消息的负担。若本来想让人比较行动，却用记牌难度挡住了比较，就值得把已知牌摆出来。
接下来先把天气牌收起来，回到基本版：每一步都花一块木板，桌上没有秘密。即使什么都知道，准备得更多也未必赶得上。下一章会看：木板明明够了，两只动物为什么仍可能来不及过河？
What Can I Change If I Know the Weather Earlier?

In the basic game, the plank supply, animal positions, and cost of each step were visible. The players still needed to think: a quick move now could leave them without enough planks later. What changes when something is not yet known?

Consider what Yu will do on her next turn. She might have decided without telling Lin. Or she might still be choosing between moving and collecting. These are different kinds of not knowing. In the first case, asking her could reveal an answer. In the second, there is no chosen answer yet. Guessing her decision is also different from calculating the chance of a die roll: she is considering their plans.
What Does a Face-Down Card Hide?

We will add weather to the crossing example for just one animal's action. To make the comparison clear, set up a separate moment: Hedgehog is on the starting bank, and only one plank is available. We are comparing this action, without deciding the outcome of a complete game.

Prepare six weather cards: four sunny and two rainy. Shuffle them thoroughly, draw one, and place it face down. For this action only, moving one step costs one plank in sunshine or two in rain. Without enough planks, the animal cannot move.

The drawn card already has a definite picture, although neither player has seen it. Turning it over reveals that picture; the act of revealing it does not turn sunshine into rain. If we waited until after the decision to shuffle and draw, the process generating the result would change too. Here we keep the draw the same and change only when the player sees it.

Four of the six cards make the single plank sufficient. Two do not. After a thorough shuffle, the chance of drawing sunshine is four out of six. That is the probability here. It describes possible results, without guaranteeing what this draw will produce.
Say “I'll Move,” Then Check the Weather
In the first arrangement, Yu chooses her action before turning the card over. Suppose she chooses to move.

With a sunny card, she spends the plank and moves Hedgehog onto the first stone. With rain, she needs two planks but has only one. The move fails: Hedgehog stays on the bank and the plank remains available. However, the turn is used up. Yu cannot change to collecting.
That last rule matters. Otherwise, one player might assume a failed move does not count, while the other thinks choosing it uses the turn. They would be playing different versions.

Yu could also choose to collect from the outset, keeping Hedgehog on the bank and bringing the supply to three. We have followed what happens if she chooses the risky move. Not knowing the weather does not force her to take that risk.
Check the Weather, Then Choose

The second arrangement moves the reveal earlier. After seeing sunshine, Yu can move Hedgehog to the first stone for one plank. After seeing rain, she can collect instead, staying on the bank and increasing the supply to three.

The weather cards and movement costs are unchanged. Rain still prevents her from moving with a single plank. What changes is that she has not yet committed this turn to an action, so she can choose in response to the weather.

Compare the two arrangements under the same rainy result. Committing to move leaves Hedgehog on the bank with one plank. Seeing rain and then choosing to collect leaves Hedgehog on the same bank with three. Ending in the same place does not mean the turn has produced the same result.

Knowing earlier helps here because of a specific opportunity: Hedgehog is still on the bank and can collect. Suppose it were already on a stone with one plank. In rain, it could neither move nor collect. Seeing rain and waiting might leave the same situation as choosing to move and failing. Additional information needs an available action before it gives someone a different result they can bring about.
Misunderstanding a Rule Is Another Problem

Suppose the card is face up and everyone can see rain, but Yu thinks moving still costs one plank. She is not missing the weather information; she has misunderstood the cost. Revealing another card would not fix that. The two-plank cost needs to be explained first.

When someone says, “I have no idea what to do,” follow the action closely. Has something already happened that they cannot see? Has somebody not decided yet? Or is the explanation unclear? The answer helps determine whether to reveal information sooner, leave an opportunity to respond, or rewrite the instruction.

To repeat this comparison from the same conditions, return the weather card, shuffle thoroughly, and draw again. Without replacement, the numbers of sunny and rainy cards change, so the chances may change too. We cannot change the drawing procedure while treating the deck as the same six cards.

For example, after drawing a sunny card without returning it, the remaining five cards contain three sunny cards and two rainy ones. The next chance of sunshine is three out of five. Keeping the drawn card face up lets everyone check; turning it face down may require everyone to remember what they saw. The drawing procedure stays the same, but the effort of remembering or checking information changes. If the intended challenge is comparing actions, leaving known cards visible can keep memory demands from getting in the way.

Now put the weather cards away and return to the basic version: each step costs one plank, and nothing on the table is secret. Even with everything known, collecting more might not get the animals across in time. The next chapter asks why having enough planks can still leave them too late.
木板够了，为什么还是来不及？
把上一章的天气变化放下，我们回到最初那条河。小兔和小刺猬都在起点，中央有四块共用木板。每次前进花一块；留在起点收集，可以增加两块。小林先行动，小雨再行动，四轮之内要让两只都到对岸。
前面我们已经看见，太早一起离岸会让木板不够用。那是不是多收集一些，就一定更保险？先别急着往桌上增加木板。让我们跟着它从哪里来、花到哪里，再看看为了收集而留在岸边的动物。
木板多了，是谁做了一件事？
开局四块，每用一块搭桥，中央就少一块。收集则从另外备好的材料里拿来两块新木板，加入中央；不能从旁边已经花掉的木板中取回。备用纸片够用，只是在帮我们表示新取得的木板，不算玩家已经拥有的资源。增加两块，需要有一名玩家用掉一次行动；木板不会因为过了一轮就自己出现。
第一章里，小兔先前进一步，把四块用成三块。小刺猬随后收集两块，中央变成五块。如果只比较轮末和开局，我们会看到“多了一块”，却看不见期间曾经用掉一块、又补进两块。
这就是为什么要分别问“现在有多少”和“刚才怎样变化”。现在有五块，不能告诉我们是谁留在岸边，也不能告诉我们还剩几次行动。桌游中，我们常把这类可以获得、花掉、留到以后使用的东西叫作“资源”。木板是本例的一种资源；认识这个词以后，还要继续追问它的具体用途。
拿到更多木板的目的，是把两只动物送过去。它们各需要前进三次，一共要用六块。开局只有四块，所以至少需要收集一次；这次收集增加的两块，正好补上差额。
同一只动物收集两次，会怎样？
现在设想另一种走法。第一轮，小兔前进，小刺猬收集，中央剩五块。第二轮，小兔再次前进，小刺猬又留在岸边收集，中央这次有六块。木板看起来比原来的成功路线更充足，小刺猬却还没出发。
第二轮已经结束，小刺猬只剩第三、第四轮的两次行动机会。从起点到对岸要走三步，两次机会最多只能让它走到第二块石头。即使小兔在第三轮顺利到岸，也没办法替小刺猬多走一次。
把余下的行动走完，会发生很直观的事：第三轮小兔到岸，小刺猬走上第一块石头；第四轮小兔等待，小刺猬走上第二块。中央还剩三块木板，游戏却因为四轮用完而失败。
缺少的不是材料，而是小刺猬来得及使用材料的机会。两块新木板确实拿到了，只是为了拿它们，小刺猬少走了一步。多出来的东西没有补回那一步。
这里要看清“同一只动物收集两次”。如果两人各收集一次，每只都还剩三次前进机会，仍可能在四轮内过河；我们不能把任何第二次收集都叫作失败原因。
把全队的行动加起来，也容易漏掉这个限制。六次前进加一次收集，总共七次；四轮给两人八次机会，看起来还多一次。然而小兔的空闲回合不能转给小刺猬。刚才失败的走法里，小兔第四轮等待，小刺猬仍少一次前进。我们既要算全队要做多少事，也要看每件事必须由谁来做。
结束时间也在改变一个动作的用途
现在只改一条规则：允许五轮，其余照旧，备用纸片也按新轮数备足。刚才停在第二块石头的小刺猬，就可以在第五轮用一块木板到岸。同样的收集次数、同样的路线，因为多了一轮，原本赶不上的计划能够完成了。
反过来，只给三轮会怎样？每只动物都需要三次前进，三次行动机会全得用在走路上，没有谁能腾出一次收集。初始四块又不够支付六步。因此，保持其他基本规则不变时，三轮版没有成功的走法。不能把这样的失败解释成“玩家没有想出好办法”。
我们通常会先想到给动物多少木板，最后再补一句“玩四轮”。但这句结束规则从一开始就在影响选择。想在四轮内过河，每只动物至多能用一次行动做前进以外的事；五轮给了更多余地；三轮则把原本必要的准备挤掉了。
这并不自动告诉我们应该选几轮。设计者还要决定，希望这一小段要求怎样的安排。我们现在能说明的是：改变期限，就改变了哪些计划来得及完成，不能只把它看成少玩或多玩几分钟。
剩下的木板，到底有什么用？
回到四轮基本版。第四轮轮到小雨时，假如小刺猬已经在第二块石头上，中央有一块木板，它这一回合前进就能到岸。再多三块木板不会让这一只动物更“到岸”；规则也没有给余下木板计分。
这提醒我们，物品的价值要和眼前要完成的事一起看。缺材料时，一次收集能够留下通路；缺行动时，同样的收集可能拖延到达。判断时至少要把动物位置、可用木板和剩余回合放在同一段推理里。
下一章会让这两个代价更直接地碰在一起：如果地图多一条短路，只需要走两步，却每步花两块木板，我们愿不愿意多花材料，换少走一步？木板和时间的关系，将变成地图上能看见的两条路。
Why Can We Have Enough Planks but Still Run Out of Time?

Set aside the weather variation and return to the original river. Rabbit and Hedgehog start on the bank with four shared planks. Each step costs one plank. Staying on the starting bank to collect adds two. Lin acts before Yu, and both animals must reach the far bank within four rounds.

We have seen that leaving the starting bank together too early can leave them short of planks. Would collecting more always make the crossing safer? Before adding to the supply, let's follow where the planks come from and where they go—and watch the animal staying behind to obtain them.
More Planks Mean Someone Took an Action

Collecting takes two new planks from the spare pieces; it never retrieves planks already spent. Enough spare pieces represent the new planks the rules allow. They are not resources the players already own.

The supply starts at four. Each bridge uses one, reducing that supply. Collecting brings two new planks from extra materials into the middle. A player must spend an action to add them; a new round does not make them appear automatically.

In the first chapter, Rabbit moved first, reducing four to three. Hedgehog then collected two, bringing the supply to five. Comparing only the beginning and end of the round would tell us “one more plank,” while hiding the one spent and the two gained.

We therefore need to ask both “How many are here now?” and “What changed?” Five planks do not tell us who stayed on the bank or how many turns remain. In games, things that can be obtained, spent, and saved for later use are often called resources. Planks are one resource here. After learning the name, we still need to ask what they are for.

The reason to get more is to move both animals across. Each needs three forward moves, requiring six planks altogether. They start with four, so at least one collecting action is necessary. The two planks it adds exactly cover the shortage.
What If One Animal Collects Twice?

Imagine another sequence. In round one, Rabbit moves and Hedgehog collects, leaving five planks. In round two, Rabbit moves again while Hedgehog stays on the bank to collect again. Six planks are now available. That looks more comfortable than the original successful route, but Hedgehog has not set out.

Two rounds have finished. Hedgehog has only its third- and fourth-round turns left. Crossing from the start requires three steps; two turns can take it only as far as the second stone. Rabbit might reach the far bank in the third round, but it cannot give Hedgehog an extra move.

Follow the remaining turns. In round three, Rabbit arrives and Hedgehog reaches the first stone. In round four, Rabbit waits and Hedgehog reaches the second. Three planks remain, but the four-round deadline ends the game in a loss.

What is missing is an opportunity for Hedgehog to use the material in time. The extra two planks really were obtained. Obtaining them, however, replaced a step forward. More material did not restore that step.

Notice that this is about the same animal collecting twice. If both players collect once each, each animal still has three turns for moving and can finish within four rounds. We cannot call every second collecting action a cause of failure.

Adding up the team’s actions can also hide this limit. Six moves and one collect action require seven turns in total; four rounds offer eight. Yet Rabbit cannot give its unused turn to Hedgehog. In the failed sequence, Rabbit waits in round four while Hedgehog still needs another move. We need to count both how much the team must do and which animal must do each part.
The Ending Changes What an Action Can Do

Now change one rule: allow five rounds, with everything else unchanged and enough spare paper pieces for the longer game. Hedgehog, left on the second stone, can spend a plank to arrive in the fifth round. The same collecting actions and route can now finish because another round is available.

What if we allow only three? Each animal needs three forward moves, using all three of its turns. Neither can spare a turn to collect, yet four starting planks cannot pay for six moves. With the other basic rules unchanged, the three-round version has no successful sequence. That loss cannot be explained by players failing to discover a clever enough plan.

We might choose how many planks the animals receive, then add “play four rounds” at the end. But the ending rule affects choices from the start. To finish in four rounds, each animal can spend at most one turn on something other than moving. Five rounds allow more room. Three remove the preparation the crossing requires.

This does not automatically tell us how many rounds to choose. The designer still needs to decide what kind of planning this example should invite. We can now explain a definite consequence: changing the deadline changes which plans can be completed. It does more than add or remove a few minutes.
What Are the Remaining Planks Worth?

Return to the four-round basic version. Suppose Hedgehog begins its fourth-round turn on the second stone, with one plank available. Moving will take it across. Three additional planks would not make this animal more completely across, and unused planks earn no points.

An object's value depends on what needs to happen. When material is missing, collecting can keep a route possible. When turns are missing, the same action can delay arrival. To judge it, we need to consider animal positions, available planks, and remaining turns together.

The next chapter puts those two costs side by side on the map. Suppose a new route takes only two steps but costs two planks per step. Would we spend more material to take one fewer step? The relationship between planks and time will become two visible routes.
多一条路，选择会怎样变？
上一章里，小兔和小刺猬想一起过河，既要有木板，也要赶得上四轮的期限。沿原来的踏脚石走，每只动物要前进三次，花三块木板。现在，一个新点子出现了：如果能多花一点木板，换一条少走一步的路呢？
两条路，两种花费
这一章只给基本版增加一条路：起点岸经过小岛，再到对岸。去小岛和离开小岛各算一次前进，每次花两块共用木板。原来的踏脚石路线保持不变。两路只在起点岸和对岸相接，中途不能换路；依然只能向前走，两只动物也仍可以停在同一处，不会互相挡路。
于是，起点岸前面出现了这样的比较：
路线 · 需要几次前进 · 一共花几块木板
起点岸→第一块石头→第二块石头→对岸 · 3次 · 3块
起点岸→小岛→对岸 · 2次 · 4块
小岛路线省下一次行动，却多用一块木板。这两个数字要一起看。只说“短路更快”，容易漏掉还在中央等着两人使用的木板；只说“原路更省”，又容易忘记每只动物只有四次行动机会。
省下一步，会花在哪里？
设想比较两种开局安排。小兔先收集一次，再沿石头走，要用掉自己的四次机会：一次收集，三次前进。如果它先收集一次，再走小岛，则只用三次：一次收集，两次前进。单看小兔，它能早一点到岸。
但木板不是小兔独享的。两只都走原路，要花六块；一只走小岛、一只走原路，就要花七块。开局的四块加上一次收集得到的两块，总共只有六块。省下的小兔行动，并没有替全队补出缺少的第七块。
这时新路线把问题接回了上一章：还需要谁收集，收集后又来不来得及？例如，小兔前两轮都收集，后两轮走小岛；小刺猬第一轮等待，后面三轮沿石头前进。按这些规则，两只都能在第四轮到岸，总共拿过八块木板，用掉七块。小兔若同样收集两次却走原路，就只剩两次前进机会，走不完三步。
这里的新选择很具体：多用木板，能让收集过两次的动物仍赶上期限。它并不说明走小岛总值得，更不说明两条路已经一样好。要比较的是这次多花的木板，是否换来了全队需要的那一步。
画得近，不一定走得近
假如把小岛画得贴近起点岸，却保留“每步两块木板”的标记，花费不会因此减少。把第二块石头画得靠近对岸，也不会让小兔自动跳过它。玩家能怎么走，取决于哪些位置相连，以及走一段要付什么。
这就是阅读游戏地图时所说的“连接”。真实地图可能用纸上的距离表示路程；这个过河例子用一段连接表示一次前进，不拿尺量棋子移动了多远。
画法仍然重要。如果一条装饰性的水纹恰好像道路，新读者可能以为能沿它走。让两条路线清楚分开，把每步的木板花费放在对应连线旁边，就能帮助人看出：两步的路比较费木板，三步的路比较费行动。
同一位置，不等于互相争抢
小刺猬到了第一块石头，并不会把石头占为己有。小兔随后也可以到那里。基本版和这一章的加路变体都没有“每处只能站一只”的限制，不能因为图上画了一个小圆圈，就替规则加上阻挡。
两人仍然互相影响，因为走路用的是同一堆木板。小兔花两块去小岛，会让小刺猬可用的木板少两块；小刺猬留在岸上收集，又会增加小兔可用的木板。地图让人看见各自走到哪里，共用木板把这些路上的决定联系起来。
如果后来真要限制一块石头只能站一只，还得继续说明：另一只不能进入，还是可以多付木板进入？谁先离开，才能给别人腾地方？这些答案会直接改变可行路线，不能只在地图上画一个“1”就算讲完。当前规则明确允许同处，因此刚才的木板和行动计算里没有额外的占位费用。
这条小岛路线暂时留在本章。下一章回到原来的两块踏脚石，继续问一个与路线相连的问题：两人都想用中央的木板时，谁先行动，会改变他们怎样计划？
How Does Another Route Change the Choice?

In the previous chapter, Rabbit and Hedgehog needed both enough planks and enough time to cross together. The original stepping-stone route takes each animal three moves and three planks. Here is a new idea: could spending an extra plank let an animal take one fewer step?
Two routes, two kinds of cost

For this chapter, add just one route to the base game: starting bank to island to far bank. Reaching the island and leaving it each take one move, costing two shared planks each time. The stepping-stone route stays unchanged. The routes meet only at the banks, so animals cannot switch halfway across. Movement remains forward only, and both animals may share any location. Neither blocks the other.
The choice at the starting bank now looks like this:
Route · Moves needed · Total planks spent
Starting bank → first stone → second stone → far bank · 3 · 3
Starting bank → island → far bank · 2 · 4

The island route saves one action but spends one extra plank. Both numbers matter. Calling it faster can hide its extra demand on the shared supply. Calling the original route cheaper can hide the fact that each animal has only four chances to act.
Where does the saved action go?

Compare two opening plans. Rabbit could collect once, then take the stepping stones. That uses all four of Rabbit’s chances: one collecting action and three moves. Collecting once and taking the island uses only three: one collecting action and two moves. Looking just at Rabbit, the island allows an earlier arrival.

But Rabbit does not have a private supply. Taking both animals along the original route costs six planks. Sending one by the island and the other by the stones costs seven. The four starting planks plus the two from one collecting action make only six. Saving Rabbit an action has not supplied the team’s missing seventh plank.

The route therefore brings back the previous chapter’s question: who will collect again, and can that animal still arrive in time? For example, Rabbit could collect in each of the first two rounds and take the island in the last two. Hedgehog could wait in the first round, then make its three moves along the stones. Under these rules, both reach the far bank in round four. The team has obtained eight planks and spent seven. If Rabbit collected twice but took the original route, it would have only two chances left for a journey requiring three moves.

The extra route offers a specific possibility: an animal that collects twice can still meet the deadline by spending more planks. That does not make the island worthwhile in every situation or show that the routes are equally strong. The useful comparison is whether the extra plank buys a step the team needs.
Close in the picture is not always close in play

Suppose we draw the island beside the starting bank but keep the two-plank labels on its route. Its cost does not fall. Drawing the second stone closer to the far bank does not let Rabbit skip it. Permitted journeys depend on which places connect and what it costs to travel between them.

Those links are the map’s connections. A real-world map might use drawn distance to represent travel distance. This example uses one connection to represent one move. Nobody measures how far a piece slides across the paper.

The drawing still matters. A decorative ripple might look like a path, encouraging a newcomer to follow a connection that does not exist. Separating the routes clearly and placing each plank cost beside its link can help someone see the choice: two moves cost more planks; three moves cost more actions.
Sharing a place does not mean competing for it

When Hedgehog reaches the first stone, it does not claim the stone. Rabbit may join it later. Neither the base game nor this chapter’s extra-route version limits a location to one animal. A small circle in the picture does not introduce a blocking rule.

The players still affect one another because they spend from the same pile. Rabbit’s two-plank move to the island leaves two fewer planks for Hedgehog. Hedgehog collecting at the bank adds planks Rabbit can use. The map shows their separate journeys; the shared supply connects the decisions they make along them.

If a later version allows only one animal on a stone, it needs further answers. Is the other animal forbidden to enter, or may it pay more planks to enter? Who must leave to make room? These answers change possible routes; a “1” drawn on the map would not explain them. The current rules explicitly allow sharing, so the calculations above contain no extra cost for occupying a place.

We leave the island route in this chapter. The next chapter returns to the original two stepping stones and follows a related question: when both players want the shared planks, how does acting first change the way they plan?
轮到别人时，我在等什么？
上一章增加的小岛路线先收起来。现在回到基本版：两块踏脚石，每步一块木板，每轮小林先行动，小雨后行动。地图告诉我们能往哪里走，回合顺序告诉我们谁先改变这张地图和中央的木板。
后行动的人，看见了什么？
第一轮，小林让小兔前进，中央的木板从四块变成三块。轮到小雨时，小兔已经站在第一块石头上。小雨可以结合这个结果决定让小刺猬做什么：如果也前进，两只都会离开唯一能收集木板的起点岸；如果收集，中央就会增加到五块。
两人当然可以在小林行动前商量。可是，“我打算前进”和“小兔已经前进”仍有区别。前者还可以改变，后者已经花掉一次机会和一块木板。后行动的人是在已经发生的结果上接着决定。
小林也不是只需要顾自己的那一步。他若打算前进，就要考虑小雨之后是否愿意收集。两人共用目标和木板，一个人的打算会用到另一个人的行动机会。因此，小雨还没动棋子时，也可能正在认真看小兔往哪里走。
如果每轮商量谁先呢？
现在只改一条规则：每轮开始先商量谁先行动，然后两人仍各行动一次。其他规则保持基本版。
第一轮可以让小雨先收集，中央从四块变成六块，再让小林前进，剩五块。这个轮末结果，与小林先前进、小雨再收集相同：小兔在第一块石头，小刺猬在岸上，中央五块木板。
结果相同，决定的顺序却不同。小林这次移动前，已经看见木板补上了；原来的安排里，小林先用掉木板，小雨再接着处理。选谁先行动，让“由谁先把计划做出来”也成为两人要商量的事。
增加自选顺序，也不能补好所有局面。比如两只动物第一、第二轮都前进，第二轮末便同在第二块石头，中央木板为零。它们都离开了可以收集的起点。第三轮即使重新商量谁先，也没有人能补木板，更没有人能先走一步。顺序要通过某个能改变后续条件的动作才产生帮助；把同样做不成的两次前进调换，并没有修好材料短缺。
不过，这多了一次讨论。若每轮都重问谁先，可能打断原本很顺的轮流节奏。对于这个小例子，我们已经看见一种能成功的固定顺序；允许改变顺序有什么用，还得看它能解决什么具体困难，不能只因为多了选择就认定更好。
同时决定，不等于同时完成
再把刚才的变体放下，另看一种：两人可以先商量，然后各自秘密选好本轮的一项行动，一起揭示。揭示后仍先执行小林的行动，再执行小雨的；木板不够的前进会变为等待，用掉本轮机会，也不能改选。这样，“选哪一项”和“实际做出来”就分成了两步。
设想只看这样一轮：小兔在第二块石头，小刺猬在第一块石头，中央只剩一块木板。两人都选前进。按刚写的处理办法，小兔先花掉木板到岸，小刺猬随后没有木板，只能留在原处。这不是说合作的人一定会如此选择，而是说明规则必须能处理这种选择。
若改成“发生冲突后重新商量”，又会多出一个决定。若把优先权给小雨，则会是小刺猬前进、小兔留下。同样的两张选择，执行办法不同，桌上的结果也不同。这里仅比较这一轮，不声称这些处理能挽救整个局面。
所以，把“大家一起选”写进规则之后，事情还没有交代完。先选、揭示、执行分别发生在什么时候，尤其是共用物品不够时，要让每个人知道下一步。
等待也可能是计划的一部分
回到基本版那条成功路线。第三轮小兔先到对岸，小刺猬随后到第二块石头。第四轮轮到小林，只能等待；小雨再花最后一块木板，把小刺猬送到岸上，两人一起获胜。
小林这次等待，不是因为不知道规则，也不是被小刺猬挡住。他的动物已经完成路程，全队还差队友的一步。小林可能期待最后一只动物到岸，也可能觉得结尾已经确定，想赶快开始下一局。仅看见他没有动棋子，还不足以判断这段时间对他意味着什么。
设计回合时，要同时看玩家什么时候能行动，以及不能行动时还有什么值得理解或关注。顺序让我们看清谁先花了木板、谁随后补入木板。下一章就沿着这堆木板继续追：它们从哪里来，经过哪些步骤，又为什么离开可用的一堆？
What Am I Waiting For on Someone Else’s Turn?

Put aside the island route from the previous chapter. We are back to the base game: two stepping stones, one plank per move, Lin acting before Yu each round. The map tells us where movement is allowed. Turn order tells us who first changes the positions and the shared supply.
What does the second player get to see?

In round one, Lin moves Rabbit forward, reducing the supply from four planks to three. When Yu’s turn begins, Rabbit is already on the first stone. Yu can decide what Hedgehog should do in response to that result. Moving would leave both animals away from the only place where collecting is allowed. Collecting would bring the supply up to five.

The players can discuss their plans before Lin acts. Even so, “I intend to move” differs from “Rabbit has moved.” The intention can still change. The completed move has already used an action and a plank. The second player continues from something that has happened.

Lin also needs to think beyond Rabbit’s own step. A plan to move may depend on Yu being willing to collect afterward. With a shared goal and shared planks, one person’s plan can depend on the other’s opportunity to act. Yu may therefore be following Rabbit closely before moving a piece.
What if they choose who goes first?
Change just one rule: at the start of each round, the players agree who acts first. Each still takes one action. Everything else stays as in the base game.

They could have Yu collect first in round one, increasing the supply from four to six. Lin then moves, leaving five planks. The round ends in exactly the same position as when Lin moves before Yu collects: Rabbit on the first stone, Hedgehog at the bank, and five shared planks.

The result matches, but the order of the decisions differs. This time Lin sees the extra planks before moving. In the original arrangement, Lin spends a plank before Yu follows through. Choosing the first player makes “Who carries out our plan first?” another matter for discussion.

Choosing the order cannot repair every position. If both animals move in rounds one and two, both end round two on the second stone with no planks. Both have left the starting bank where collecting is possible. Even if they choose who goes first in round three, neither can add planks or move. Order helps through an action that changes the conditions for a later action. Reordering two moves that remain impossible does not repair the shortage.

That also adds a conversation. Reconsidering the order every round could interrupt an otherwise straightforward rhythm. We already know a successful plan using the fixed order. To understand the value of a flexible order, we need to identify a difficulty it addresses, rather than treating an extra choice as an automatic improvement.
Choosing together is not finishing together

Set that variation aside and consider a separate one. The players may discuss, then secretly select one action each and reveal together. After the reveal, Lin’s action happens first and Yu’s second. A move that cannot be paid for becomes a wait, uses that player’s opportunity for the round, and cannot be replaced with another choice. Selecting an action and carrying it out are now separate steps.

Look at one round with Rabbit on the second stone, Hedgehog on the first, and only one shared plank. Both players choose to move. Under the procedure just described, Rabbit spends the plank and reaches the far bank. Hedgehog then has no plank and stays where it is. This does not predict that cooperating players will choose this combination. It explains what the rules must do if they do.

Allowing another discussion after a clash would add a decision. Giving Yu priority instead would move Hedgehog and leave Rabbit in place. The selected actions are the same, but the order in which they happen changes the result. We are comparing this round only, not claiming that these procedures rescue the whole position.

Writing “Everyone chooses together” therefore leaves something unfinished. Players need to know when they choose, when choices become visible, and how actions happen—especially when there is not enough of a shared item for every plan.
Waiting can belong to the plan

Return to the successful route in the base game. In round three, Rabbit reaches the far bank first; Hedgehog then reaches the second stone. In round four, Lin can only wait. Yu spends the final plank, moves Hedgehog to the far bank, and both players win together.

Lin is not waiting because the rules are confusing or Hedgehog blocks the way. Rabbit has completed its journey, and the team needs one more step from its partner. Lin might look forward to that arrival. Or the ending may feel settled already, leaving Lin ready for another game. Seeing no piece move is not enough to tell us what the interval means to that player.

When designing turns, consider when players can act and what remains worth understanding or following when they cannot. Order helps us see who spends planks first and who adds them afterward. The next chapter follows this pile further: where do its planks come from, what steps do they pass through, and why do they leave the available supply?
木板从哪里来，又到哪里去？
上一章里，小雨先收集，小林移动之前就看见了新增的木板。顺序让我们看清材料何时到来。不过，木板是怎样进入中央的？用过以后还能再拿回来吗？这些事情也要由规则决定。
先回到基本版：开局四块共用木板，收集从备用纸片取得两块新木板，前进花掉一块，把它放到已用的一旁。两只动物要在四轮内各走三步，合作到岸。这一章先保持目标和期限，追踪支持行动的东西。
有进有出，不一定绕一圈
中央是玩家现在能花的木板。备用纸片表示尚未取得的材料，已用木板表示已经付出的费用。三处虽然都放着相似的纸片，作用却不同。
第一轮小兔前进、小刺猬收集：中央先由四变三，再由三变五。用掉的那一块仍在旁边，新加入的两块来自备用。木板从获得到使用，走的是一条路；规则没有让它们回到中央。
如果收集改成“从已用堆拿回两块”，就变成另一种来源。开局已用堆为空，没人花过木板时便拿不回任何东西。基本版能在第一回合直接收集，新办法却必须等先有人花费。看起来同样是中央增加两块，能不能开始、何时能做，已经不同。
给资源安排来源和去处，是设计游戏经济的一部分。这里的“经济”不要求有钱或买卖：只要木板能被获得、保留、使用，它怎样支持行动就值得追踪。
原料多了，为什么成品没有更多？
现在单独看动物出发前的一个河岸准备片段。它不接在基本版之前，也不给后面的过河游戏额外木板。我们只比较准备工作：两轮内做出四块成品木板，达到四块立即完成，否则第二轮结束便未完成。
小林、小雨每轮仍依次各行动一次，共四次机会。开始没有原木，也没有成品，两人共用材料。每次可以收集两根新原木；或者消耗两根原木，锯成两块成品木板；也可以等待。原木不足两根不能锯。原料供应充足，没有其他费用，也不在这段中移动动物。
第一轮小林收集，得到两根原木；小雨锯木，原木变零，成品变两块。第二轮重复这两个动作，成品到四块，完成。原木与成品不能混在一起数：两根尚未加工的原木，不能当作两块已完成的木板。
假如只把每次收集提高到三根，会快一点吗？第一轮收集后有三根，锯完剩一根原木、两块成品。第二轮再收集，原木到四根；再锯，最后是两根原木、四块成品。仍然用了四次行动，成品也仍是四块。
增加收集数量，增加的是等待加工的东西。两次锯木每次只能做两块，限制了这一计划的成品数量。这个卡住后续工作的环节，可以叫“瓶颈”。我们已经有足够原料时，再增加原料，并没有增加加工机会。
改哪里，才会影响眼前的问题？
只把锯木改成“花三根，做三块”，也不能立刻解决它。回到每次只收集两根的安排，第一次收集后连新费用都付不起，还得再花一次行动凑原料。生产多少与需要多少，必须接得上。
如果同时改成每次收集四根，锯木消耗四根、做四块，那么第一轮两次行动就能完成原定目标。这说明怎样让它更快，却也拿掉了原来第二轮的安排。设计者若想让两人商量怎样分工，不能只看成品数增加了，还要看新的速度是否让想要的过程消失。
这些规则把一项“取得木板”拆成了收集与加工。拆开后能比较先准备什么，也要多记一类物品、多说明一次转换。如果希望读者只关注谁留在岸边帮忙，基本版的一步收集已经足够；只有加工顺序本身值得比较时，多一堆原木才承担了工作。
增加数量，什么时候会越长越快？
让东西增加，还可以不靠玩家主动收集。例如，另设一条补给规则，每次补给固定加入两块木板。补给前有三块，就变五块；有六块，就变八块。存得多，没有让这次补给给得更多。
再独立比较一种补给办法：补给开始时，每满三块现有木板就获得一块新木板，只计算一次。开始有三块，得到一块，变四块；开始有六块，得到两块，变八块。数量较多会带来更多新增，新增又能帮助以后达到更多的三块。这种把增长接回增长条件的关系，叫正反馈。这里仅比较补给步骤，没有把它加入前面的准备或过河规则。
同样是木板越来越多，固定补给与按存量补给的原因不同。后者可能让保留木板有额外好处；但木板若最终要用于过河，留着不花也可能耽误出发。要判断这条关系有没有用，还得把获得的好处接回目标与期限，而不能只赞成“增长更快”。
现在把原木和补给变体收起来，回到基本版。木板支持动物前进，收集要占用行动，四轮决定还来不来得及。沿着来源、加工、使用追踪一遍，我们能找到该改哪一步。下一章再改那个一直保留的条件：一局究竟要争取什么，又在什么时候停下来？
Where Do Planks Come From, and Where Do They Go?

In the previous chapter, Yu collected first, so Lin saw the additional planks before moving. Order helped us follow when material arrived. But how do planks enter the shared supply? Can spent planks be taken back? The rules must determine these things too.

Return first to the basic game: four shared planks at the start; collecting takes two new planks from spare pieces; moving spends one and puts it aside as used. Both animals must make three moves within four rounds and reach the far bank together. We will first keep this goal and deadline while following the things that support their actions.
Things Can Enter and Leave Without Going Around

The central pile contains planks the players can spend now. Spare pieces represent material not yet obtained; the used pile represents costs already paid. The pieces may look alike, but the three places mean different things.

In round one, Rabbit moves and Hedgehog collects. The central pile goes from four to three, then from three to five. The spent plank stays aside. The two added planks come from the spares. Planks follow a path from acquisition to use; no rule returns them to the middle.

Changing collect to “take two planks back from the used pile” would create a different source. The used pile starts empty, so nothing can return before someone spends a plank. Basic collecting works on the very first turn; the new version would have to wait for spending. Both may look like adding two planks, but they differ in when the action can begin and when it is available.

Deciding where resources come from and go is part of designing a game economy. An economy does not require money or shopping here. If planks can be obtained, kept, and used, their connection to actions is worth following.
Why Might More Raw Material Produce No More Finished Planks?

Consider a separate preparation scene on the bank before the animals set out. It is not a new stage attached to the basic game and gives no extra planks to a later crossing. We compare only preparation: make four finished planks within two rounds. Reaching four completes the task immediately; otherwise it is incomplete at the end of round two.

Lin and Yu still take one turn each per round, in that order, for four turns altogether. They start with no logs and no finished planks, and share all materials. On a turn, a player may collect two new logs, consume two logs to saw them into two finished planks, or wait. Sawing requires two logs. Raw material is plentiful, there are no other costs, and the animals do not move during this scene.

In round one, Lin collects two logs. Yu saws them, leaving no logs and two finished planks. Repeating those actions in round two reaches four planks and completes the task. Raw and finished material must be counted separately: two unprocessed logs are not two completed planks.
